candidateRows: A cumulative historical case can make belief in Jesus' resurrection reasonable by identifying likely facts and comparing explanations for them.
This supplies the governing method for the entire affirmative case: establish historical facts and then determine which proposed explanation best accounts for them.
After introducing his experiential and evidential reasons for Christianity, Mike defines the historical-fact and best-explanation structure that organizes his resurrection defense.
Jesus' death by Roman crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is among the most securely supported facts relevant to the resurrection case.
Jesus' death is a necessary foundation for any resurrection inference and is presented as the first component of the affirmative's cumulative historical case.
Mike transitions from explaining his method to enumerating twelve proposed historical facts, beginning with the Roman crucifixion and its asserted multiple attestation.
Jesus was probably buried in a private tomb that was later found empty, with multiple independent considerations supporting the empty-tomb account.
The claimed empty tomb is a principal element of the affirmative's historical footprint and materially narrows explanations based only on subjective experiences.
Mike acknowledges comparatively lower scholarly support for burial and the empty tomb, then argues from multiple attestation, enemy attestation, women witnesses, Joseph, and archaeology.
The disciples had individual and group experiences they understood as appearances of the risen Jesus, making ordinary hallucination an inadequate explanation.
Post-death appearance experiences are direct explanatory data for the resurrection hypothesis and anchor the affirmative's rejection of a principal naturalistic rival.
Following the empty-tomb discussion, Mike cites individual and group appearance traditions, early sources, and scholarly statements before arguing that group hallucinations do not fit.
The disciples' transformed lives and willingness to endure persecution show that they sincerely believed they had encountered the risen Jesus.
The sincerity inference is essential to excluding deliberate conspiracy and connects the claimed appearances to the subsequent conduct of the earliest witnesses.
Mike argues that persecution and martyrdom, especially involving Peter, James, and Paul, place the claimed witnesses in a position to know and indicate sincere conviction.
Early public resurrection preaching in Jerusalem and the resurrection's centrality to the gospel weigh against late legend or deliberate fabrication.
The timing, location, and central content of the proclamation are used to make the claims locally testable and to reverse the proposed direction of legendary development.
Mike combines early proclamation, its Jerusalem setting, and the resurrection-centered message to argue that belief in the resurrection generated the church rather than vice versa.
The religious and prophetic context surrounding Jesus indicates that, if he rose, the event is best understood as an act of God.
This move bridges the historical claim that Jesus rose and the supernatural causal conclusion required for the affirmative's specifically Christian explanation.
Mike describes Jesus as a miracle worker, exorcist, prophetic agent, and apparent fulfiller of scripture, then connects that setting to divine causation of the resurrection.
James changed from a skeptic during Jesus' life into an early church leader after an experience he took to be an appearance of the risen Jesus.
James's asserted conversion provides an additional hostile-or-skeptical witness whose change the resurrection hypothesis is offered to explain independently of the disciples.
After arguing from religious context, Mike presents James's prior unbelief, later leadership, reported appearance, and the claimed broad scholarly acceptance of his conversion.
Paul's conversion and suffering followed an experience he believed was an appearance of the risen Christ, adding another independently attested transformation.
Paul supplies another former opponent whose conversion and costly commitment require explanation within the affirmative's cumulative historical argument.
Mike concludes his list with the former persecutor Paul, his reported appearance experience and suffering, then characterizes the full set as nonmiraculous common ground.
The resurrection explains the cumulative historical data better than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, or combinations of those rival explanations.
This is the affirmative's principal abductive inference, converting the preceding historical claims into the conclusion that resurrection belief is reasonable.
After establishing his proposed common ground, Mike argues that resurrection fits the data while conspiracy, hallucination, legend, and hybrid theories inherit unresolved problems.
Even sincere testimony about an extraordinary experience supplies a claim, not sufficient evidence that the supernatural explanation is true.
This distinction establishes the skeptical evidential framework Matt applies throughout his case against treating resurrection reports as adequate proof.
Mike's opening treated the reported experiences and historical assertions as cumulative evidence supporting the resurrection.

After distinguishing reasonableness from truth, Matt uses his honest mother's demon report to argue that sincerity can justify accepting that an experience occurred without accepting its supernatural interpretation.
Mike's cited material consists largely of resurrection claims rather than independent evidence, while legend remains a natural candidate explanation preferable to an unsupported supernatural one.
It directly contests the evidential status of the pro case and preserves a natural rival explanation, addressing the central reasonableness question.
Mike characterized the collected historical reports as evidence and dismissed legend as an irresponsible explanation of the facts.

Matt says evaluation requires separating claims from evidence, argues that reports of appearances are themselves claims, and counters that invoking supernatural causation is less responsible than considering legend.
Resurrection is inadmissible as the best explanation unless its possibility and supernatural mechanism are independently supported rather than specially exempted from ordinary evidential standards.
The move directly challenges whether supernatural resurrection can reasonably enter the explanatory comparison without prior evidence that it is possible.
Mike presented resurrection as the explanation that best accounts for the collected historical claims and rejected excluding supernatural causation in advance.

Matt argues that no comparable resurrection has been evidenced, reality appears inconsistent with such events, and supernatural interaction must first be demonstrated before it can serve as an explanation.

Known natural causes such as deception, legend, error, and exaggeration outrank resurrection as candidates because resurrection lacks independent support, and Hume's test favors rejecting the less probable account.
It supplies the comparative explanatory rule by which the con side prefers documented natural phenomena over an otherwise unsupported miraculous cause.
Mike compared rival explanations and argued that the cumulative first-century data make an actual resurrection the superior explanation.
Matt demands a known mechanism, lists familiar natural sources of erroneous reports, denies that resurrection belongs in the candidate set without support, and invokes the greater-miracle comparison.

Not knowing in advance what evidence would establish resurrection expresses epistemic humility rather than closed-mindedness, because sufficient evidence could still convince him and an omniscient God could provide it.
The move answers a credibility challenge to the skeptical standard and preserves the con position as evidentially open rather than unfalsifiable by definition.
Mike argued that Matt's inability to specify what evidence would convince him was effectively an admission that nothing could convince him.

Matt distinguishes inability to predict a decisive test from refusal to accept evidence, citing the unprecedented and untestable character of supernatural resurrection while affirming that adequate evidence would persuade him.

The resurrection case relies on noncontemporary, source-dependent claims whose contradictions and uncertain reliability prevent the minimal-facts list from being treated as established historical facts.
It attacks the historical foundation of the cumulative case by disputing contemporaneity, independence, consistency, and the conversion of reported claims into facts.
Mike offered numerous historical sources and a cumulative list of facts, while maintaining that the Gospel accounts do not materially contradict one another.

Matt argues that the cited writings postdate the events, that prior supernatural assumptions distort plausibility, and that Gospel inconsistency matters because the Bible supplies claims rather than independent evidence.

Choosing resurrection after dismissing selected natural alternatives commits an argument from incredulity because unknown possibilities and incomplete information remain, leaving insufficient evidence and 'I don't know' as the warranted conclusion.
It synthesizes the con case against inference to resurrection and states the ultimate burden conclusion that belief is unreasonable on the available information.
Mike argued that legend, conspiracy, and other rivals fail to explain the cumulative evidence, leaving resurrection as the explanation that best fits the data.

Matt characterizes the sources as uninvestigable reports, labels elimination-to-resurrection reasoning Doyle's fallacy, illustrates limited-information error, and concludes that unknown causes are preferable to an unsupported supernatural assertion.
Archaeological confirmation that first-century tomb descriptions match ordinary local tombs establishes only accurate background detail, not the burial, named participants, or resurrection narrative.
The reply tests a specific category of pro evidence and argues that authentic setting details do not corroborate the disputed central events of a narrative.
Mike asked Matt to define the distinction between claims and evidence after objecting to Matt's repeated denial that the resurrection case contained evidence.

Matt defines a claim as an assertion and evidence as support for its truth, then compares accurate tomb-setting details to future discovery of New York buildings being treated as evidence for Spider-Man.

If an archaeologically impossible tomb description would count against the account, a fitting tomb, burial agent, cultural context, and archaeological setting should correspondingly increase its likelihood.
It defends the cumulative method by arguing that contextual archaeological fit has positive corroborative force even if it does not independently prove resurrection.
Matt argued that archaeologically accurate descriptions of ordinary first-century tombs establish only mundane setting details and do not support the burial account.

Mike asks Matt to concede that a physically impossible tomb would disconfirm the narrative, then argues that the observed fit of the tomb, attributed burier, context, and archaeology should count in the opposite direction.
Confirming that a narrative correctly mentions ordinary period details can rule out certain errors without supplying positive evidence that its extraordinary transaction or central event occurred.
This response directly addresses asymmetric corroboration and explains why mundane contextual accuracy does not materially verify the extraordinary proposition under debate.
Mike argued that because archaeological mismatch would disconfirm the tomb account, archaeological and contextual fit should make the reported burial more likely.

Matt compares the tomb argument to a future researcher verifying that dollars existed: absence would disconfirm the story, but existence confirms only incidental historical accuracy, not the alleged transfer of money.
Detailed knowledge of Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs cumulatively corroborates the historical reliability of gospel reporting.
This supplies a central bridge from mundane historical accuracy to the claimed credibility of the testimonial sources underlying the resurrection case.
Matt's claim that accurate mundane details do not corroborate the central events narrated in a story.
After Matt distinguishes period accuracy from proof of a transaction, Mike argues that numerous locally specific details should be assessed cumulatively rather than dismissed as mere claims.
Accuracy concerning some elements of a narrative does not establish the truth of its independent resurrection claims.
The move attacks the inferential link between verified background details and the extraordinary proposition that the debate asks the sources to support.
Mike's argument that accumulated accurate local details make the gospel accounts and their central claims more credible.
Matt separates confirmation of incidental narrative details from confirmation of other claims, maintaining that independently framed propositions require their own support.
A two-part case combining reasonably established historical facts with resurrection as their best explanation is not defeated by a categorical demand to prove the conclusion first.
This states the affirmative's overarching inferential structure and challenges the skeptical standard alleged to prevent any evidence from establishing resurrection.
Matt's contention that the resurrection claims fail a sound epistemic standard and have not been adequately demonstrated.
Mike distinguishes the historical-fact component from the explanatory component, then argues that Matt rejects the very evidence that could establish the disputed conclusion.
Concluding that resurrection has not met its burden is neither circular nor equivalent to assuming that supernatural events cannot occur.
The move defines the con side's central burden-based position while distinguishing nonacceptance from a positive claim that resurrection was impossible or did not occur.
Mike's accusation that Matt's evidential standard circularly prevents resurrection evidence from ever proving resurrection.
Matt explains the formal character of circular reasoning, disclaims conclusions of impossibility or nonoccurrence, and locates the failure in the affirmative's unmet burden.
The reported crucifixion lacks contemporary verification, while absent independent reports of associated extraordinary events undermine confidence in the narrative source.
This directly contests the historical foundation of the affirmative's first-stage case by challenging both source contemporaneity and expected external corroboration.
Mike's request that Matt accept Jesus' crucifixion under Pontius Pilate as one of the historical facts in the two-part case.
While reviewing the proposed historical facts, Matt says he cannot investigate the account through contemporary records and points to missing reports of conspicuous associated phenomena.
Paul's language and relevant Jewish historical concepts indicate that he understood Jesus to have undergone a bodily rather than merely spectral resurrection.
Paul's understanding is important to whether the earliest cited testimony concerns a physical resurrection, strengthening the affirmative's characterization of the testimonial claim.
Matt's characterization of the Damascus-road encounter as a vision involving no visibly present physical person.
Mike shifts from the Acts encounter narrative to Pauline resurrection language, appearance traditions, and historical semantics to argue for a bodily-resurrection understanding.
Paul's beliefs and reports about appearances are third-party claims that neither establish the cited witnesses' attestations nor show that resurrection occurred.
This isolates the skeptical case's key distinction between reports of belief and warranted belief in the event, directly challenging the affirmative's testimonial inference.
Mike's reliance on Paul and reported appearances to James, the Twelve, and others as support for a bodily resurrection.
Matt argues that Paul speaks for absent third parties, that their own confirmation is unavailable, and that sincere belief would still not establish the event's truth.
A gospel author's report that adversaries acknowledged a fact is not independent enemy attestation unless an actual adversarial source supplies the acknowledgment.
The argument challenges a specific claimed line of independent support for the empty tomb and clarifies the source-independence standard governing testimonial corroboration.
Mike's opening claim that Matthew 28 provides enemy attestation supporting the empty-tomb account.
Matt contends that treating a favorable author's portrayal of opponents as their independent testimony assumes the very reporting accuracy that requires support.
Roman burial protocol requiring a confirmatory piercing of crucifixion victims corroborates the spear detail as historically normal rather than a later exaggeration.
The move supports Jesus' confirmed death and the historical reliability of a disputed narrative detail, both relevant to excluding survival-based rival explanations.
Matt's suggestion that the spear and blood-and-water material could have been added after the fact to make death seem certain.
Mike invokes an external description of Roman practice to argue that piercing before burial fits ordinary protocol and therefore need not be an apologetic embellishment.
Describing ordinary historical and medical facts as evidence specifically for Jesus can smuggle the disputed conclusion into otherwise mundane corroboration.
This generalizes the con side's core objection that background compatibility is repeatedly presented as event-specific support without independently establishing the contested occurrence.
Mike's presentation of Roman piercing practice and medical explanations for blood and water as corroboration of Jesus' reported wound and death.
Matt accepts that crucifixion, stabbing, and relevant physiology were real while arguing that imprecise phrasing improperly turns such commonplace facts into case-specific support.
Even directly observing Jesus return to life would not by itself establish either supernatural causation or divine agency.
This separates evidence that a person became alive again from the further causal claim that God raised him, directly testing the motion's supernatural inference.
Mike's hypothetical that a presently observed and scientifically confirmed return to life would warrant belief that God raised Jesus.
Mike proposes a modern, directly observable death-and-return scenario; Matt answers that even establishing renewed life would leave its cause unresolved and criticizes the historical timing.
The resurrection case fails because its available support is insufficient for an extraordinary claim, not because evidence is irrelevant to skepticism.
The move states the skeptical burden test at the center of the debate and applies it directly to the absence of physical, contemporary, and possibility-establishing support.
Mike's characterization that Matt's inability to specify decisive evidence shows that evidence effectively does not matter to him.
After an interruption dispute, Matt distinguishes openness to evidence from accepting inadequate support and argues that the claimed resurrection bears an unusually demanding evidential burden.
Requiring extraordinary evidence is circular because any extraordinary support offered can itself be redescribed as another extraordinary claim needing further support.
The argument attacks the governing evidential standard used by the skeptical side, so its success would materially alter how the resurrection case must be supported.
Matt's claim that extraordinary claims require evidence proportionate to their extraordinariness and that the resurrection lacks such support.
Following Matt's insistence on extraordinary support, Mike argues that the standard creates an endless regress in which no proposed support can enter consideration as adequate.
Evidence proportionate to an extraordinary claim need not become a new unsupported claim; it can instead be sufficient confirmation of the original claim.
This directly answers the alleged regress and preserves the skeptical principle that warrant depends on evidence rising to the improbability or extraordinariness of a claim.
Mike's regress argument that extraordinary evidence would always count as a further extraordinary claim requiring still more extraordinary evidence.
Matt rejects the claimed circularity, reformulates the principle in terms of sufficient warrant, and uses confirmation of a winning lottery claim to explain the distinction.
The quantity and quality of required support should scale with how extraordinary a claim is and must overcome well-supported beliefs that conflict with it.
The move supplies the affirmative rationale for applying a higher burden to resurrection testimony and connects that burden to the claim's implications for an entire worldview.
Mike's attempt to classify ordinary verification, such as matching lottery numbers, as enough to support an extraordinary outcome.

Continuing the dispute over extraordinary evidence, Matt contrasts low-stakes mundane claims with resurrection and argues that warrant must account for both improbability and contrary background knowledge.
Reconstructing a more coherent first-century story cannot establish its truth, while a message-bearing God would be responsible for making adequate evidence accessible.
This answers the demand for a rival historical reconstruction while shifting the evidential responsibility to the hypothesized divine communicator whose message allegedly matters universally.
Mike's request that Matt investigate first-century circumstances and provide a specific, thoughtful alternative explanation for the reported evidence.
Matt says contextual history may improve narrative consistency without proving the narrative and argues that a just God should ensure the evidence needed for reasonable acceptance is available.
Beginning with Christian belief and later finding historical material consistent with it reverses sound inquiry, which should follow evidence before adopting the conclusion.
The move challenges the reliability of the pro side's belief-formation process and argues that prior supernatural commitments can make virtually any later observation appear consistent.
Mike's account of first becoming Christian through personal experience and subsequently discovering historical support that reinforced his prior conviction.

After Mike cites personal experience and later historical confirmation, Matt argues that belief-first investigation invites confirmation bias and describes abandoning his own earlier faith when support proved insufficient.
The first century was strategically suited to spread the resurrection message because shared language, Roman travel networks, codex adoption, and later population growth amplified transmission.
The move directly counters the objection that divine action occurred at an evidentially poor time by offering a positive historical rationale for choosing that period.
The skeptical objection that placing the resurrection two millennia ago, before cameras and modern investigation, made the event arbitrarily difficult to verify.

Asked why the resurrection allegedly occurred without modern recording technology, Mike doubts cameras would resolve skepticism and argues that first-century communication infrastructure favored broad dissemination.
Testimony can count as evidence without being sufficient, and the resurrection reports are especially limited because they are noncontemporary and transmitted second- or third-hand.
This directly evaluates the principal testimonial foundation of the resurrection case and explains why attestation volume does not by itself warrant the historical or supernatural conclusion.
The questioner's suggestion that testimony's accepted evidential role in modern courts supports treating the reported resurrection testimony as adequate evidence.
Matt concedes that testimony is a recognized evidential category but argues that belief counts and sincerity do not determine truth, while the relevant reports lack contemporary first-hand status.

The resurrection belief is unreasonable because much of the offered support is unremarkable and comes through a selectively assembled scriptural collection rather than independently decisive confirmation.
This is Matt's closing synthesis of why the affirmative's cited facts and multiple attestations do not meet the motion's burden, including concerns about scriptural selection and preservation.
Mike's broader case that the presented historical facts and multiple scriptural attestations make belief in Jesus' resurrection reasonable.

Matt begins his closing by returning to the precise motion, rejecting the expectation that every alleged fact requires direct denial, and characterizing much of the affirmative case as evidentially unremarkable.
Even the most accurate surviving biblical record would not establish that its resurrection account is accurate or sufficiently evidenced for present belief.
This challenges the inference from multiple canonical attestations and comparative textual accuracy to the reasonableness of accepting the resurrection claim.
Mike's appeal to multiple sources and historical attestations as evidence supporting the resurrection.
Matt argues that the canon was assembled by people who excluded competing works and that even maximal record accuracy would not supply adequate warrant for belief today.
Christianity's post-crucifixion growth required belief in the resurrection or belief that others believed it, not an actual resurrection.
It supplies a rival causal account of the movement's revival, undermining the claim that actual resurrection is the best explanation of its expansion.
Mike's claim that the movement's renewed expansion after Jesus' death is best explained by an actual resurrection.
Matt concedes that a resurrection could explain the movement's growth but argues that sincere transmission of resurrection belief would explain the same historical development.
The ending and later additions to Mark expose unresolved textual problems in the resurrection narratives and their transmission.
The argument uses a concrete textual discrepancy in an early Gospel to contest the reliability and coherence of the testimonial basis for resurrection belief.
Mike's reliance on early testimonial material and multiple historical sources for the resurrection case.
Matt says the apostles need not have lied, then contrasts Mark's earliest ending with its later verses and asks how the conflicting reports about the women can be reconciled.
Textual problems and the absence of evidence beyond resurrection reports make suspension of judgment more reasonable than accepting resurrection as an explanation.
It directly answers the debate's reasonableness question by connecting deficiencies in the evidence to a positive case for withholding assent.
Mike's conclusion that the supplied historical considerations make resurrection the best available explanation.
Matt characterizes the narrative issues as real problems, stresses that only reports rather than independent physical evidence are available, and endorses admitting uncertainty.
If God raised Jesus and expects belief, God bears responsibility for ensuring that people receive evidence sufficient to warrant that belief.
It relocates the evidential burden from the skeptic to the asserted divine agent and makes evidential sufficiency central to reasonable belief.
The suggestion that skeptical nonbelief persists despite evidence that should already be sufficient for accepting the resurrection.
After endorsing uncertainty about the reports, Matt argues conditionally that a God responsible for the resurrection must also provide adequate grounds for accepting it.
Confirming an unusual event would not establish supernatural causation, which cannot be inferred merely by eliminating other proposed causes.
It directly challenges the decisive inference from historical phenomena to divine resurrection and states a prerequisite for treating the supernatural as explanatory.
Mike's inference that the historical facts favor supernatural resurrection after rival natural explanations are judged inadequate.
Matt rejects portrayals of his skepticism as personal stubbornness and distinguishes evidence for an event from evidence identifying a supernatural cause of that event.
The resurrection case rests on ordinary historical methods and scholarly evidence rather than requiring a prior defense of complete Gospel reliability.
It restates the affirmative methodology and conclusion, presenting resurrection as the best explanation under familiar standards of historical inquiry.
Matt's criticism of canonical selection, Gospel textual reliability, and the sufficiency of biblical resurrection reports.
Mike clarifies that his case used explanatory power, explanatory scope, early and multiple sources, archaeology, and majority scholarship before reaffirming his conclusion.
Open-ended skeptical questions do not defeat the resurrection case when they lack supported alternative explanations and adequate historical grounding.
This attacks the adequacy of the negative case by arguing that unexplained possibilities and questions carry insufficient force against an explanatory argument.
Matt's use of unresolved questions and possible narrative or natural alternatives to resist the resurrection explanation.
Mike summarizes Matt's approach as casting doubt through questions without defending historical alternatives and argues that this does not seriously engage the evidence.
The deeper disagreement is epistemological: whether one is sufficiently open to allowing the historical evidence to support the conclusion that Jesus rose.
It identifies the debate's controlling methodological dispute and explains why the parties interpret the same claimed evidence differently.
Matt's methodological refusal to treat supernatural resurrection as an available candidate explanation from the historical evidence.
Mike says the greater issue is epistemology rather than a complete rehash of individual facts and proposes that openness to the evidential conclusion needs separate discussion.
First-century evidence supports Jesus' resurrection, and accumulated modern historical research places present investigators in an especially strong position to assess it.
It directly affirms the evidential reasonableness of resurrection belief and counters the contention that temporal distance prevents adequate investigation.
Matt's claim that surviving reports do not provide people today with sufficient evidence to warrant resurrection belief.
Mike argues that first-century material favors resurrection and that collected data and extensive historical study enable thoughtful contemporary evaluation of Jesus' death and resurrection.
